summary30s: The Harappan (Indus Valley) Civilisation flourished c. 2600-1900 BCE (Mature Harappan phase), distinguished by standardized grid-pattern urban planning and burnt-brick drainage.
Settlements were divided into a raised Western Citadel (for public/ritual functions: Great Bath, Warehouse) and a lower Eastern Town (residential quarters).
Specialized craft centers included Chanhudaro (bead-making, shell-cutting, seal-making) and Lothal, utilizing carnelian, lapis lazuli (Shortughai), copper (Khetri), and steatite.
The Harappan script remains undeciphered; it was written right-to-left (boustrophedon tendencies), logo-syllabic with 375-400 signs, found on seals, copper tablets, and jars.
Subsistence combined domestic agriculture (wheat, barley, lentils, sesame; rice at Lothal/Rangpur) and animal husbandry, supplemented by copper and chert stone blade technology.

coreConcepts.title: Planned Urban Layout: Citadel and Lower Town
coreConcepts.explanation: Mohenjodaro exemplifies Harappan urbanism. The settlement is divided into two distinct sectors: the elevated Citadel (built on mud-brick platforms, walled, housing elite/civic structures like the Great Bath and Warehouse) and the Lower Town (residential sector). Roads cut each other at right angles in a strict grid pattern. Every house had its own bathroom paved with bricks, connected through wall channels directly into street drains.
coreConcepts.ncertPointer: Themes in Indian History Part I, Section 2: 'Mohenjodaro A Planned Urban Centre'
coreConcepts.examTip: CUET frequently asks: 'The Great Bath was made watertight by setting bricks on edge and using mortar of gypsum.' Remember gypsum mortar was used for waterproofing.

coreConcepts.title: Craft Production and Raw Material Procurement
coreConcepts.explanation: Chanhudaro was an almost exclusively specialized craft production center (less than 7 hectares) focused on bead-making, shell-cutting, seal-making, and weight-making. Specialized drills were discovered at Chanhudaro, Lothal, and Dholavira. Raw materials were procured through distant trade and colonies: Lapis lazuli from Shortughai (Afghanistan); Carnelian from Bharuch (Gujarat); Steatite from South Rajasthan and North Gujarat; Copper from Khetri region of Rajasthan (Ganeshwar-Jodhpura culture) and Oman (Magan); Gold from South India (Kolar).
coreConcepts.ncertPointer: Themes in Indian History Part I, Section 4 & 5
coreConcepts.examTip: Mesopotamian texts refer to Meluhha (land of seafarers / Harappan region), Dilmun (Bahrain), and Magan (Oman).

coreConcepts.title: Subsistence Strategies and Agricultural Technology
coreConcepts.explanation: Archaeo-botanists identify wheat, barley, lentil, chickpea, and sesame. Millets are found in Gujarat sites; rice finds are rare. Animal bones include cattle, sheep, goat, buffalo, and pig (domesticated) alongside wild species (boar, deer, gharial). Agricultural technology utilized oxen for ploughing: terracotta models of the plough were found at Cholistan and Banawali (Haryana); evidence of a ploughed field with two perpendicular sets of furrows was excavated at Kalibangan (Rajasthan). Canals have been traced at Shortughai (Afghanistan), but not in Punjab or Sindh.
coreConcepts.ncertPointer: Themes in Indian History Part I, Section 1
coreConcepts.examTip: Water reservoirs carved in stone for agricultural runoff were found at Dholavira (Gujarat).

coreConcepts.title: The Undeciphered Script, Weights, and Social Structure
coreConcepts.explanation: The Harappan script has 375 to 400 distinct signs and is non-alphabetical (logo-syllabic). It was written right-to-left, proven by wide spacing on the right and cramping on the left of seal edges. Weights followed a binary system at lower denominations (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 up to 12,800) and decimal system for higher denominations. Cubical chert weights had no markings. Regarding governance, theories range from a single ruler ('Priest-King' statue of Mohenjodaro) to equal multiple states or community consensus, though a centralized single state best explains standardized brick ratios (1:2:4) across hundreds of miles.
coreConcepts.ncertPointer: Themes in Indian History Part I, Section 6 & 7
coreConcepts.examTip: Standard brick ratio throughout the Mature Harappan culture was 1 : 2 : 4 (Thickness : Breadth : Length).

workedExamples.question:
Match List-I (Harappan Sites) with List-II (Specialized Evidence / Discoveries):
List-I:
(A) Kalibangan
(B) Shortughai
(C) Chanhudaro
(D) Dholavira

List-II:
1. Traces of canals
2. Water reservoirs
3. Ploughed field surface with two furrow grids
4. Exclusive craft production and bead factory
workedExamples.explanation: Kalibangan shows the earliest ploughed field (two sets of furrows at right angles, suggesting two crops grown together). Shortughai in Afghanistan has evidence of irrigation canals. Chanhudaro was dedicated almost entirely to craft production (bead-making). Dholavira features elaborate stone-cut water harvesting reservoirs.
solutionStepByStep: Step 1: Identify Kalibangan -> ploughed field evidence (Pair A with 3).
Step 2: Identify Shortughai in Afghanistan -> traces of canals found in rocky/semi-arid terrain (Pair B with 1).
Step 3: Identify Chanhudaro -> bead-making workshops and drills (Pair C with 4).
Step 4: Identify Dholavira -> monumental water reservoirs (Pair D with 2).
Conclusion: Option A (A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2) is correct.
workedExamples.cuetPattern: Match-the-following site association is the single most recurring question format in CUET History Theme 1.
solutionSteps: Step 1: Identify Kalibangan -> ploughed field evidence (Pair A with 3).
Step 2: Identify Shortughai in Afghanistan -> traces of canals found in rocky/semi-arid terrain (Pair B with 1).
Step 3: Identify Chanhudaro -> bead-making workshops and drills (Pair C with 4).
Step 4: Identify Dholavira -> monumental water reservoirs (Pair D with 2).
Conclusion: Option A (A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2) is correct.

workedExamples.question:
Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R):
Assertion (A): Harappan domestic architecture demonstrated an extraordinary concern for individual privacy.
Reason (R): Houses in Mohenjodaro had no windows in the walls along the ground level, and the main entrance did not give a direct view of the interior or courtyard.

options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)

workedExamples.explanation: According to NCERT Theme 1 Section 2, residential buildings in the Lower Town centered on a courtyard. There were no windows in walls at ground level to prevent outsiders from peeking, and doorways were positioned so as not to afford direct visual access to inner courtyards. Thus (R) directly explains (A).
solutionStepByStep: Step 1: Evaluate Assertion (A): True. NCERT states explicitly that privacy was a marked feature of Harappan homes.
Step 2: Evaluate Reason (R): True. Wall construction omitted ground-level windows, and entrances were angled.
Step 3: Establish causal link: The absence of windows and indirect entryway were intentional architectural mechanisms designed to guarantee privacy.
Conclusion: Both are true and (R) correctly explains (A). Option A is correct.
workedExamples.cuetPattern: CUET assertion-reason questions frequently test subtle NCERT architectural and societal observations.
solutionSteps: Step 1: Evaluate Assertion (A): True. NCERT states explicitly that privacy was a marked feature of Harappan homes.
Step 2: Evaluate Reason (R): True. Wall construction omitted ground-level windows, and entrances were angled.
Step 3: Establish causal link: The absence of windows and indirect entryway were intentional architectural mechanisms designed to guarantee privacy.
Conclusion: Both are true and (R) correctly explains (A). Option A is correct.

howCuetAsks.typicalStem: Arrange the following archaeologists in chronological order of their work on Harappa: (i) R.E.M. Wheeler, (ii) Alexander Cunningham, (iii) John Marshall, (iv) Daya Ram Sahni.
howCuetAsks.strategy: Memorize: Cunningham (1875) -> Sahni (1921) -> Marshall (1924 announcement) -> Wheeler (1944 Director General of ASI).

howCuetAsks.typicalStem: Which of the following regions was called 'Meluhha' in Mesopotamian texts?
howCuetAsks.strategy: Meluhha = Harappan region; Magan = Oman (source of copper); Dilmun = Bahrain island.

commonTraps.misconception: Students often assume canals were excavated in Harappa and Mohenjodaro (Punjab and Sindh).
commonTraps.correctConcept: Canals were only found at Shortughai (Afghanistan). In Punjab and Sindh, irrigation was primarily drawn from wells.
commonTraps.whyTrapWorks: Options list Punjab or Sindh alongside Shortughai, causing confusion due to the proximity of Indus river tributaries.
commonTraps.cuetWarning: Always pick Shortughai for canal traces; pick Dholavira for reservoirs.

commonTraps.misconception: Believing iron tools were used in Mature Harappan craft and agriculture.
commonTraps.correctConcept: Harappans were in the Bronze Age. Iron was completely unknown to Harappans; it appeared in India c. 1000 BCE.
commonTraps.whyTrapWorks: Questions ask 'Which of the following metals was NOT known to the Harappans?' and options include Copper, Bronze, Gold, and Iron.
commonTraps.cuetWarning: Iron is ALWAYS the correct answer for metals unknown to Harappans.

practiceQuestions.question: Terracotta models of the plough have been discovered by archaeologists at which of the following Harappan sites?
practiceQuestions.explanation: According to NCERT Theme 1, terracotta models of the plough have been found at sites in Cholistan and at Banawali (Haryana).

practiceQuestions.question: Which of the following materials was used to make the Great Bath at Mohenjodaro watertight?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The Great Bath was made watertight by setting bricks on edge and using a mortar of gypsum (Themes in Indian History Part I, p. 7).

practiceQuestions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding Harappan weights:
I. The lower denominations of weights were binary (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32).
II. The higher denominations followed the decimal system.
III. Weights were made of a stone called steatite and were generally spherical.
Which of the above statements are correct?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Statements I and II are correct. Statement III is incorrect because weights were made of chert (not steatite) and were cubical (not spherical) with no markings.

practiceQuestions.question:
Match the raw material in List-I with its Harappan procurement location in List-II:
List-I:
(A) Copper
(B) Lapis Lazuli
(C) Carnelian
(D) Gold

List-II:
1. South India (Kolar)
2. Khetri region of Rajasthan
3. Shortughai (Afghanistan)
4. Bharuch (Gujarat)
practiceQuestions.explanation: Copper came from Khetri (Rajasthan) and Oman; Lapis Lazuli from Shortughai; Carnelian from Bharuch; Gold from South India.

practiceQuestions.question: Which of the following Director Generals of the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) brought military precision and stratigraphy techniques to Harappan excavations in 1944?
practiceQuestions.explanation: R.E.M. Wheeler took over as Director-General of the ASI in 1944 and recognized that it was necessary to follow the stratigraphy of the mound rather than dig horizontally along mechanical levels.

practiceQuestions.question:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: The Harappan script was written from right to left.
Statement II: Some Harappan seals show wider spacing on the left and cramping on the right, proving scribes started on the left.

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true

practiceQuestions.explanation: Statement I is true. Statement II is false because the seals show wider spacing on the right and cramping on the left, proving the scribe started typing from right to left and ran out of space on the left.

practiceQuestions.question: Specialized drills used in Harappan bead-making have been excavated at which of the following sets of sites?
practiceQuestions.explanation: NCERT Theme 1 explicitly states: 'Specialised drills have been found at Chanhudaro, Lothal and more recently at Dholavira.'

practiceQuestions.question:
Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R):
Assertion (A): Cunningham, the first Director-General of the ASI, missed the historical significance of Harappa.
Reason (R): Cunningham used accounts left by 4th-7th century CE Chinese Buddhist pilgrims to locate early historic settlements, mistakenly believing Indian history began with the Ganga valley cities.

options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)

practiceQuestions.explanation: Cunningham's main interest was the archaeology of the Early Historic (c. 6th century BCE to 4th century CE) period. Because Harappa was not part of the itinerary of the Chinese pilgrims and did not fit his historical framework, he failed to realize how old it was.

practiceQuestions.question: At which of the following Harappan coastal sites were specialized shell-working industries located for making bangles, ladles, and inlays?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Nageshwar and Balakot were settlements located near the sea coast, specialized for making shell objects like bangles, ladles, and inlays.

practiceQuestions.question: What was the characteristic feature of Harappan burials in terms of social differentiation?

options.text: Massive deposits of gold and platinum were buried with kings in pyramidal mounds
Burials generally contained pottery and ornaments, reflecting a belief in an afterlife, but without lavish wealth
Complete cremation was universal; no skeletons have survived in burial pits
Only women were buried with jewellery; men were buried without any grave goods

practiceQuestions.explanation: Harappan burials were in pits containing pottery and simple ornaments (copper mirrors, shell rings). Harappans generally did not believe in burying precious things with the dead, unlike Egyptian Pharaohs.
